item.title: China Pushes Back Against U.S. on Iran and Cuba in UN Speech
item.description: By Antoni Slodkowski China pushed back against the United States in its speech at the UN General Assembly on Saturday, saying the sovereignty of countries in the Gulf should be respected and urging the “relevant country” to stop threatening Cuba and lift its blockade on …
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded:
By Antoni Slodkowski

China pushed back against the United States in its speech at the UN General Assembly on Saturday, saying the sovereignty of countries in the Gulf should be respected and urging the “relevant country” to stop threatening Cuba and lift its blockade on it.

Vice President Han Zheng did not name the US in his remarks. The US has launched a pressure campaign on Cuba that has largely blocked oil from reaching the island. The U.S. war on Iran started with U.S.-Israeli strikes in February.

The comments stood in sharp contrast to the bonhomie on display earlier this week at the White House, where President Donald Trump feted Chinese leader Xi Jinping with military flyovers and at a lavish state dinner.

“Major countries should have special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security, and they should take the lead in complying with the rules, upholding the rule of law, and doing what’s right,” Han said.

“China holds that the sovereignty and security of countries in the Middle East, including the Gulf, should be respected.”

Trump warned Xi against supporting Iran during the Washington talks and received assurances that China would not do so, the US ambassador to China said on Friday.

The warning followed reports that Beijing had supplied Iran with shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers and that Tehran had found ways to evade sanctions on its oil sales with Chinese help.

Call for End of Blockade on Cuba

On Cuba, Han said: “China urges the relevant country to immediately stop using the threat of force against Cuba and immediately and completely lift the blockade and sanctions against Cuba.”

Cuba’s electrical grid suffered a total collapse earlier this month, plunging the nation into darkness and leaving millions without power as the US presses its blockade.

Cuba’s aging power generation system has been under severe strain from fuel shortages and decrepit infrastructure for years, but a US-imposed oil blockade that began in January has worsened blackouts and led to frequent grid collapses.

Han also used the speech to portray China as a reliable partner on the global stage and a steadfast defender of developing nations.

“China holds that all countries, big or small, are equal members of the international community, and that world affairs should be handled by all through consultation,” said Han.

item.title: A Lapel Pin Fuels Chinese Talk of a China-Russia-Iran Triangle
item.description: In China’s tightly managed political information environment, seemingly trivial interactions between senior officials can become material for close reading. Netizens and commentators scrutinize seconds-long clips — who smiles, who initiates a handshake, how firmly leaders grip hands or whether they appear unusually relaxed around one …
item.dc:creator: Rudy Lu
item.content:encoded:
In China’s tightly managed political information environment, seemingly trivial interactions between senior officials can become material for close reading. Netizens and commentators scrutinize seconds-long clips — who smiles, who initiates a handshake, how firmly leaders grip hands or whether they appear unusually relaxed around one another — for clues about relationships that official readouts rarely reveal.

A brief encounter between the foreign ministers of China, Russia and Iran at the BRICS summit has become the latest example.

Video from the sidelines of the summit in New Delhi showed Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi chatting and laughing with his Russian and Iranian counterparts Sergei Lavrov and Abbas Araghchi. At one point, Wang reached toward a pin on Araghchi’s jacket, prompting the Iranian foreign minister to laugh.

Araghchi’s official Telegram channel later posted a close-up of the exchange , identifying the pin as an emblem depicting the map of Iran.

The moment quickly spread across Chinese social media, landing on the trending search list of Weibo, a Chinese social media platform often compared to X, under “Wang Yi helps the Iranian foreign minister straighten his pin” (#王毅帮伊朗外长整理胸针).

A wave of Chinese-language amplification followed.

Nationalist commentary account Rongping (戎评) described Iran as “holding the advantage” and in high spirits, with China and Russia sharing the mood.

“Such a personal and warm interaction between the Chinese and Iranian foreign ministers sends a strong signal to the outside world: China-Iran relations have long gone beyond a simple exchange of interests, and the two sides share a high degree of familiarity and trust,” it wrote.

Another online commentary said the seemingly insignificant gesture reflected a shift in the international balance of power that would make the White House “deeply uncomfortable.”

“U.S. pressure is pushing the three sides closer together,” it said. “Washington can continue to pressure the three countries separately, but it will find it increasingly difficult to stop them from exchanging resources, coordinating positions and jointly seeking alternatives.”

It said Beijing could keep channels open to Gulf Arab countries, and Moscow could draw on its close strategic ties with Tehran. Working through BRICS, the three could help Iran break its diplomatic isolation and avert a complete rupture with the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf states.

Those interpretations, however, largely reflect one strand of domestic online opinion that is sympathetic to Iran and distrustful of the United States. Beijing’s official posture has been more carefully calibrated, especially ahead of Xi Jinping’s scheduled Sept. 24 meeting with Trump in Washington.

Araghchi traveled to Beijing on Sep. 16 for talks with Wang Yi. The Chinese Foreign Ministry described Iran as a “comprehensive strategic partner” and said Beijing was prepared to help safeguard Tehran’s “legitimate rights and interests.”

But much of Wang’s message focused on containing the conflict. He urged Iran and the United States to exercise restraint and return to negotiations, backed dialogue between Tehran and Gulf Arab governments, called for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and warned against the fighting spreading toward Yemen and the Red Sea.

China’s balancing role was also evident when Saudi Arabia asked Beijing to press Iran to rein in the Houthis, Reuters reported, citing three Iranian sources . China then privately urged Tehran to use its influence over the Yemeni group, whose advances threatened Saudi oil exports and shipping through the Red Sea — a vital route for Chinese trade.
